{{Short description|Inequality in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Maclaurin's inequality''', named after [[Colin Maclaurin]], is a refinement of the [[inequality of arithmetic and geometric means]]. 

Let <math>a_1, a_2,\ldots,a_n</math> be [[non-negative number|non-negative]] [[real number]]s, and for <math>k=1,2,\ldots,n</math>, define the averages <math>S_k</math> as follows:
: <math>S_k = \frac{\displaystyle \sum_{ 1\leq i_1 < \cdots < i_k \leq n}a_{i_1} a_{i_2} \cdots a_{i_k}}{\displaystyle {n \choose k}}.</math>

The numerator of this fraction is the [[elementary symmetric polynomial]] of degree <math>k</math> in the <math>n</math> variables <math>a_1, a_2,\ldots,a_n</math>, that is, the sum of all products of <math>k</math> of the numbers <math>a_1, a_2,\ldots,a_n</math> with the indices in increasing order. The denominator is the number of terms in the numerator, the [[binomial coefficient]] <math>\tbinom n k.</math> Maclaurin's inequality is the following chain of [[inequality (mathematics)|inequalities]]:

: <math display="inline">S_1 \geq \sqrt{S_2} \geq \sqrt[3]{S_3} \geq \cdots \geq \sqrt[n]{S_n}</math>,

with equality [[if and only if]] all the <math>a_i</math> are equal.

Maclaurin's inequality can be proved using [[Newton's inequalities]] or a generalised version of [[Bernoulli's inequality]].

== Examples ==

For <math>n=2</math>, Maclaurin's inequality gives the [[arithmetic mean-geometric mean inequality]] for two non-negative numbers. 

For <math>n=4</math>, Maclaurin's inequality states:
: <math display>\begin{align}
&\quad \frac{a_1+a_2+a_3+a_4}{4} \\[8pt]
&\ge \sqrt{\frac{a_1a_2+a_1a_3+a_1a_4+a_2a_3+a_2a_4+a_3a_4}{6}} \\[8pt]
&\ge \sqrt[3]{\frac{a_1a_2a_3+a_1a_2a_4+a_1a_3a_4+a_2a_3a_4}{4}} \\[8pt]
&\ge \sqrt[4]{a_1a_2a_3a_4}.
\end{align}</math>
